definition: The d= tag of a DKIM signature: the domain that takes responsibility for the message. DMARC checks whether it aligns with the From: domain.
example: A valid signature with d=invoicer.example does not align with From: billing@corp.example in the example's unrelated-domain case.

definition: The bh= tag of a DKIM signature: a hash of the canonicalised message body (or the prefix chosen by l=). Any covered change to the body makes it mismatch.
example: Adding covered non-whitespace body text changes the canonicalised body hash; content outside an l= prefix is not covered.

definition: DKIM rules for transforming covered headers and body bytes before hashing. Relaxed mode normalises specified whitespace and header-name case; it does not excuse arbitrary text or header-value changes.
example: With relaxed, "Subject:  Hi" and "subject: Hi" hash the same.

definition: The part of an email or HTTP header before the colon, such as Subject in "Subject: Lunch?". In email it is case-insensitive.
example: "subject" and "Subject" are the same field name.

definition: An optional DKIM tag limiting the body hash to the first l bytes. Content appended after that prefix is not covered by the signature, which is a risk.
example: With l=500, a footer added after byte 500 does not break the signature.

definition: The size of a DKIM RSA key in bits. RFC 8301 requires at least 1024 bits and recommends at least 2048.
example: A 512-bit DKIM key is too weak and should be rejected.

definition: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance: a policy at _dmarc.<domain> saying a message passes only if email SPF or DKIM passes for a domain aligned with the visible From:, and what receivers should do otherwise. RFC 9989 (2026) replaces RFC 7489.
example: _dmarc.alice.example TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject" asks receivers to reject failing mail.

definition: DMARC's requirement that the domain email SPF or DKIM authenticated matches the visible From: domain: the same organisational domain in relaxed mode, exactly the same in strict mode.
example: promo.shop.example aligns with shop.example in relaxed mode but not strict.

definition: A domain boundary determined by DMARC's specified discovery procedure for comparing relaxed alignment. RFC 9989 uses DNS tree walks and policy information rather than assuming it is always a two-label registered suffix; older RFC 7489 implementations can differ.
example: mail.alice.example and alice.example share organisational domain alice.example.

definition: The two DMARC alignment modes. Relaxed (default) accepts subdomains of the same organisational domain; strict (aspf=s for email SPF, adkim=s for DKIM) needs an exact domain match.
example: With aspf=s, an email SPF pass for promo.shop.example does not align with shop.example.

definition: The DMARC p= tag requests none (no DMARC-specific enforcement), quarantine (suspicious treatment) or reject (rejection) for failing messages, subject to receiver discretion. RFC 9989 separately requires fully participating domain owners to send with both aligned email SPF and aligned DKIM, and forbids relying solely on email SPF with p=reject.
example: Enforcing reject before every legitimate source has an aligned pass can cause legitimate mail to be rejected, subject to receiver policy.

definition: A requested summary of observed sending sources and authentication/disposition results. The rua tag supplies report destinations; participation and report delivery are not guaranteed, and RFC 9990 specifies the current aggregate format.
example: Reports reveal an invoicing SaaS sending as corp.example without alignment.

definition: Sending mail that claims to come from someone else's address, usually in the From: header. Phishing uses it to impersonate banks and colleagues.
example: A phisher sends From: <it@alice.example> from their own server.

definition: Authenticated Received Chain (RFC 8617): each forwarder records the authentication results it saw and signs them, so a final receiver that trusts the forwarder can accept mail whose email SPF and DKIM broke in transit.
example: A mailing list adds ARC seals saying DKIM passed on arrival.

definition: A sender of large volumes of mail. Gmail requires senders of around 5,000 or more messages a day to personal accounts to use email SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
example: A newsletter sending 20,000 messages a day to Gmail must publish DMARC.

definition: A List-Unsubscribe mechanism (RFC 8058) that lets a recipient unsubscribe with a single click in the mail client, without visiting a website.
example: Gmail shows an Unsubscribe link next to the sender for compliant mailings.

definition: Software as a service: software run by a vendor and used over the internet, such as an invoicing or marketing tool that sends mail on your behalf.
example: An invoicing SaaS sending as billing@corp.example needs aligned DKIM.

definition: Python's standard-library module for speaking SMTP as a client.
example: smtplib.SMTP(host, 587) opens a submission connection.

definition: Microsoft's hosted office suite, including Exchange Online email for organisations.
example: A company's staff mail is sent by its Microsoft 365 tenant.

definition: One customer's separate account and data inside a shared hosted service.
example: corp.example's Microsoft 365 tenant is isolated from other companies'.

definition: Network Time Protocol: the protocol computers use to set their clocks from time servers over the network. Version 4 runs over UDP port 123.
example: An NTP client polls configured time sources and disciplines its clock. Its accuracy and polling interval depend on the implementation, sources and network.

definition: An NTP server's distance from a reference clock. Stratum 1 servers attach directly to a reference clock, stratum 2 servers sync from stratum 1, and so on; stratum 16 means unsynchronised.
example: A server syncing from a GPS-attached stratum 1 server reports itself as stratum 2.

definition: A highly accurate time source, such as a GPS receiver or an atomic clock, that a stratum 1 NTP server reads directly. It is informally called stratum 0.
example: A stratum 1 server in a data centre may take its time from a GPS antenna on the roof.

definition: NTP's estimate of server time minus client time from four timestamps, under its clock-rate and path-delay model. A positive result estimates that the client is behind; filtering, uncertainty and discipline policy determine any correction.
example: With t1 = 10.000, t2 = 10.150, t3 = 10.152 and t4 = 10.042 seconds, the offset is 0.130 s: the client is 130 ms behind.

definition: In NTP, the total time a request and its response spent on the network: the client's elapsed time minus the time the server spent processing. It bounds how wrong one offset measurement can be.
example: If 41 ms pass on the client and the server held the request for 1 ms, the delay is 40 ms.

definition: When the trip from client to server takes a different time from the trip back. NTP assumes both directions are equal, so asymmetry biases its offset estimate by half the difference.
example: A 5 ms outbound and 35 ms return trip makes NTP's offset wrong by (5 − 35) / 2 = −15 ms.

definition: The four times recorded in one NTP exchange: t1 when the client sends, t2 when the server receives, t3 when the server replies and t4 when the client receives. t1 and t4 come from the client's clock, t2 and t3 from the server's.
The gradual gain or loss of time by a clock whose oscillator runs slightly fast or slow. It is usually quoted in parts per million.
example: A clock drifting at 20 ppm gains or loses about 1.7 seconds a day.

definition: A ratio of one in a million, used to express how fast or slow a clock runs. 1 ppm is one microsecond of error per second of real time.
example: 20 ppm × 86,400 seconds in a day ≈ 1.7 seconds of error per day.

definition: The electronic component, usually a vibrating quartz crystal, that ticks at a fixed frequency to drive a computer's clock. Temperature and ageing make its frequency, and so the clock, drift slightly.
example: A typical PC quartz oscillator may be off by tens of ppm.

definition: Gradually correcting a clock offset by adjusting its rate rather than making a discontinuous step. Available rates and correction policy depend on the implementation and configuration.
example: At 500 ppm, slewing away a 1-second error takes about 2,000 seconds, roughly 33 minutes.

definition: Correcting a clock by setting it directly to the new time, so it jumps forwards or backwards. Steps can break duration measurements that use wall-clock time.
example: Classic ntpd steps the clock when the offset exceeds 128 ms, subject to safeguards.

definition: The reference NTP daemon (background program) from the Network Time Foundation, long the standard NTP implementation on Unix systems.
example: Classic ntpd uses a 128 ms step threshold by default.

definition: An NTP implementation including the chronyd daemon, with configurable clock discipline, source selection and slew behaviour. Whether a machine uses it by default depends on its distribution and installation.
example: chrony configuration determines allowed slew rates and whether an offset may be stepped.

definition: A clock that cannot go backwards or be stepped by changing wall-clock time, used to measure durations. Its epoch is unspecified; rate adjustment, resolution and whether suspension counts depend on the specific clock/platform.
example: Subtracting two time.monotonic() readings in Python gives a request's duration even if NTP stepped the wall clock in between.

definition: The ordinary date and time of day a computer reports, which NTP or an administrator can step forwards or backwards. Use it for timestamps, not for measuring durations.
example: If the wall clock is stepped back 300 ms during a 50 ms request, the measured duration is −250 ms.

definition: An adjustment to UTC used under its time-scale rules to keep it near Earth-rotation time UT1. A positive leap adds one second; CGPM Resolution 4 (2022) calls for increasing the permitted UT1–UTC difference by or before 2035 rather than specifying permanent abolition on one unconditional date.
example: A positive leap second makes the last minute of a day 61 seconds long, ending at 23:59:60.

definition: Spreading a leap second over a long period by running clocks very slightly slow or fast instead of inserting an abrupt extra second. Google smears over 24 hours centred on the leap second.
example: In Google's 24-hour smear, clocks run about 11.6 ppm slow and are 0.5 s off unsmeared UTC at the leap moment.

definition: Coordinated Universal Time: the world's standard civil time scale, based on atomic clocks and kept close to the Earth's rotation by leap seconds.
example: NTP servers distribute UTC; local time zones are offsets from it.

definition: Universal Time 1: time based on the Earth's actual rotation angle, which varies slightly. Leap seconds keep UTC within 0.9 seconds of UT1.
example: UT1−UTC is the difference that leap seconds currently keep below 0.9 s.

aliases: General Conference on Weights and Measures
Conférence générale des poids et mesures
definition: The General Conference on Weights and Measures: the international body that decides the SI units and time-scale policy. Its Resolution 4 of 2022 calls for a larger permitted UT1−UTC difference by or before 2035.
example: CGPM Resolution 4 (2022) is why leap seconds are expected to stop being inserted for a long period.

definition: Time-based One-Time Password: a code computed from a shared secret and a time step, commonly six digits with a 30-second step. Step length, digits, acceptance windows and replay prevention are configured protocol choices; the two sides need sufficiently aligned clocks.
example: An authenticator app shows a new 6-digit TOTP code every 30 seconds.

definition: A network authentication system using tickets issued by trusted services. Ticket validity and replay protection require clock handling; acceptable skew is configurable, with a 300-second default documented for MIT krb5.
example: A Windows domain login uses Kerberos tickets, so a badly drifted clock can stop users logging in.

definition: Global Positioning System: a satellite navigation system whose satellites carry atomic clocks. A GPS receiver can supply very accurate time, so it is a common reference clock.
example: A stratum 1 NTP server often takes its time from a GPS receiver.

definition: A special NTP reply with stratum field 0 that tells a client to stop or slow down, for example because it is querying too often. The reason is a four-character code in the reference ID field.
example: A server may send a RATE Kiss-o'-Death to a client polling every second.

definition: NTP timestamps count seconds since 1 January 1900 in 32 bits, which overflow after 2^32 seconds, about 136 years, in February 2036. Each 136-year span is an era, and implementations must use other date information to tell eras apart.
example: 2^32 seconds after 1 January 1900 is 7 February 2036.

definition: One trillionth of a second (10^−12 s). NTP's 32-bit fraction of a second gives a resolution of about 233 picoseconds.

Network Time Security: an extension that authenticates NTP. A TLS key-establishment phase on TCP port 4460 sets up keys, and later NTP packets carry authenticators so on-path attackers cannot forge them.
example: Cloudflare's time.cloudflare.com supports NTS so clients can detect forged time replies.

definition: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data: a cipher mode that encrypts data and also produces a tag proving it was not altered, in one operation. AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are AEADs.
example: In SSH with an AEAD cipher, the integrity check comes from the cipher's 16-byte tag rather than a separate message authentication code.

definition: A legacy ntpd query that returned a list of up to 600 recent clients. Because a small spoofed request produced a large reply, it was abused for amplification attacks (CVE-2013-5211).
example: Disabling monlist (or upgrading ntpd) removed the amplification vector.

definition: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public catalogue that gives each known security flaw a unique identifier such as CVE-2013-5211.
example: CVE-2023-48795 is the identifier for the SSH Terrapin attack.

definition: Precision Time Protocol (IEEE 1588): a clock-synchronisation protocol for local networks that can reach sub-microsecond accuracy with hardware timestamping and PTP-aware switches.
example: Stock exchanges and 5G base stations use PTP where NTP's millisecond accuracy is not enough.

definition: Recording send/receive events in network hardware near the physical interface, reducing software scheduling uncertainty. Timestamp placement, hardware calibration, path asymmetry and clock quality still limit accuracy.
example: PTP can use hardware timestamps; the timestamping feature alone does not guarantee nanosecond synchronisation.

definition: A PTP-aware network switch that measures how long each timing packet waited inside it and adds that to a correction field, so the delay does not distort synchronisation.
example: A transparent clock that held a PTP packet for 3 µs adds 3 µs to its correction field.

definition: One millionth of a second (10^−6 s).
example: One microsecond is 1,000 nanoseconds; sub-microsecond means less than that duration.

definition: Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol for logging in to remote machines, running commands and forwarding connections, normally on TCP port 22. It is three layered protocols: transport, user authentication and connection.
example: ssh alice@server.example opens an encrypted shell on server.example.

definition: SSH's layer for negotiating algorithms, performing key exchange and authenticating the server. Its binary key-exchange packets initially precede encryption; negotiated protection is activated by NEWKEYS.
example: Everything above it, including password logins, travels inside the transport layer's encryption.

definition: The first line each side sends in plaintext when an SSH connection opens, naming the protocol version and software, such as SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6.
example: SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6 advertises SSH version 2.0 and the software string OpenSSH_9.6; a banner alone does not prove the installed software version.

definition: The SSH message each side sends to list the algorithms it supports, in preference order, for key exchange, host keys, ciphers, message authentication codes and compression. The two lists decide which algorithms are used.
example: If the client lists curve25519-sha256 first and the server supports it, that key exchange is chosen.

definition: The step in which client and server agree a shared secret over an untrusted network, usually with an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange, from which session keys are derived.
example: OpenSSH 10.0's default key exchange is mlkem768x25519-sha256.

definition: A method that lets two parties each publish a value and combine it with their own secret to reach the same shared secret, which an eavesdropper cannot compute. Ephemeral means fresh secrets are used for every connection.
example: X25519 is an elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman variant used by SSH and TLS.

definition: An elliptic curve designed for fast, safe Diffie-Hellman key exchange. curve25519-sha256 is the SSH key-exchange method built on it.
example: An SSH key exchange with curve25519-sha256 sends 32-byte public values each way.

definition: A key exchange combining a classical method (X25519) with one believed to resist future quantum computers (Streamlined NTRU Prime or ML-KEM), so the result is safe if either holds.
example: OpenSSH 9.0 made sntrup761x25519 the default; OpenSSH 10.0 switched to mlkem768x25519-sha256.

definition: An SSH implementation developed by the OpenBSD project, providing clients, servers and related tools across several operating systems. Installed versions, build options and defaults vary.
example: Running ssh -V prints the installed OpenSSH version, for example OpenSSH_9.6.

definition: The long-term key pair that identifies an SSH server. The server signs each key exchange with it so the client can check it is talking to the right machine.
example: A client can compare the server host key with configured trusted keys, a known_hosts entry or a trusted host certificate authority.

definition: The file where an SSH client stores the host keys of servers it has trusted. A later mismatch triggers a loud warning because it may mean an attacker.
example: After accepting server.example once, its key line is added to ~/.ssh/known_hosts.

definition: A trusted SSH signing key used to authenticate host certificates. Clients must also check certificate validity, host principals and configured restrictions, rather than accepting every certificate carrying that signer.
example: A company configures every laptop to trust its SSH CA, so new servers need no TOFU prompt.

definition: Trust on first use: recording a previously unknown peer's key and checking future connections against it. It does not independently authenticate that first peer or make later key changes inherently illegitimate.
example: SSH's 'The authenticity of host … can't be established' prompt is a TOFU decision.

definition: A short hash of a public key or certificate, shown so humans or programs can compare keys easily. In WebRTC, a certificate fingerprint is sent in the SDP as a=fingerprint.
example: An SSH fingerprint looks like SHA256:… ; a WebRTC one like sha-256 4A:AD:B9:….

definition: A hash over the SSH key-exchange transcript and agreed secret, using the selected method's specified inputs. The server signs it and it contributes to key derivation; the first exchange hash becomes the persistent session identifier.
example: Changing any byte of the negotiation changes the exchange hash, so the server's signature no longer verifies.

definition: The exchange hash of an SSH connection's first key exchange, kept unchanged for the whole connection. Public-key logins sign it, binding the signature to this one connection.
example: A signature captured from one SSH session fails on another because their session IDs differ.

definition: The base SSH binary packet has length and padding-length fields, a payload, padding of at least four bytes and negotiated integrity protection. Base alignment counts the four-byte length field but excludes the MAC; AEAD and Encrypt-then-MAC variants alter details.
example: Check the negotiated packet construction rather than applying the base alignment rule to every SSH cipher.

definition: The SSH message that ends a key exchange; after it, each side switches to the newly negotiated keys and algorithms.
example: Strict KEX resets packet sequence numbers to zero at NEWKEYS.

definition: A short tag computed from a message and a secret key that lets the receiver detect any change to the message. HMAC-SHA2-256 is a common MAC in SSH.
example: If an attacker flips one bit of an SSH packet, its MAC check fails and the connection is dropped.

definition: An ordering in which data is encrypted first and the message authentication code is computed over the ciphertext. In SSH, the -etm@openssh.com modes use it.
example: hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com is an Encrypt-then-MAC mode; combined with CBC it was affected by Terrapin.

definition: An AEAD cipher combining the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 authenticator. It is fast in software and widely used in SSH and TLS.
example: OpenSSH often prefers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com; it was one of the modes affected by Terrapin.

definition: AES in Galois/Counter Mode: authenticated encryption combining AES encryption with an integrity tag. Some processors provide hardware acceleration; actual performance depends on hardware, implementation and workload.
example: aes256-gcm@openssh.com is an AES-GCM option in OpenSSH.

definition: Cipher Block Chaining: an older block-cipher mode in which each block is mixed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption. It needs a separate message authentication code for integrity.
example: aes128-cbc is a CBC mode; with Encrypt-then-MAC it was exposed to Terrapin.

definition: The data-block width processed by a block cipher, 16 bytes for AES. Base RFC 4253 SSH alignment includes its length field and excludes the MAC; negotiated AEAD and other packet formats need their own rules.
example: Base AES-CBC SSH packets align the specified packet portion to a 16-byte boundary.

definition: An implicit per-direction SSH packet counter, used by base RFC 4253 MACs and some negotiated constructions. SSH AES-GCM uses its own IV-based invocation counter instead; strict KEX addresses the Terrapin manipulation of affected handshake counters.
example: The initial counter begins at zero; strict KEX resets it on the specified NEWKEYS transitions.

definition: A 2023 SSH attack in which an on-path attacker injects a message during the plaintext handshake and deletes one after encryption starts, keeping sequence numbers consistent. With affected modes it silently strips extension negotiation.
example: Terrapin could delete EXT_INFO so the client never learned the server supported stronger signature options.

definition: The Terrapin fix: an SSH extension that resets sequence numbers at NEWKEYS and aborts if any unexpected message appears during the key exchange. Both client and server must support it.
example: OpenSSH 9.6 introduced strict KEX. Both peers must negotiate the extension; an older implementation may gain support through a backport.

definition: An SSH message sent straight after the key exchange that advertises protocol extensions, such as which public-key signature algorithms the server accepts.
example: Terrapin's deletion of EXT_INFO could downgrade which signature algorithms were used.

definition: The SSH service, requested inside the encrypted transport, in which the client proves who the user is using methods such as publickey or password.
example: After the transport is set up, the client requests ssh-userauth and tries its key.

definition: The SSH login method in which the client proves it holds a private key by signing data that includes the session ID. The server checks the signature against an authorised public key.
example: Listing a key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys lets its owner log in with publickey authentication.

definition: The file on an SSH server, usually ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, listing public keys allowed to log in to that account.
example: Appending a laptop's public key to authorized_keys lets it log in without a password.

definition: An SSH login method in which the server asks one or more questions and the user types answers, often used for one-time passwords.
example: A server may ask for a password and then a 6-digit code via keyboard-interactive.

definition: One-time password: a code valid for a single login or a short time, such as a 6-digit TOTP code.
example: An authenticator app's 6-digit code is an OTP.

definition: A background program that holds your private keys and signs on request, so keys never need to be read by each ssh process.
example: ssh-add loads a key into ssh-agent once; later ssh commands ask the agent to sign.

definition: An SSH feature exposing the local agent's signing service through the remote host. A sufficiently privileged remote attacker can request signatures while it is reachable, subject to confirmation, destination and hardware constraints; this does not normally export the private key.
example: With ssh -A to a bastion, a root user on the bastion could log in elsewhere as you.

definition: An SSH option that connects to a destination through an intermediate host, with the end-to-end session negotiated from your own machine, so keys never touch the intermediate host.
example: ssh -J bastion.example db.internal reaches db.internal via the bastion.

definition: A hardened host used as a controlled entry point into a private network, often for SSH access. Whether it is the only available route is a deployment decision.
example: Engineers ssh to bastion.example and from there to internal servers.

definition: An attack in which someone sits between two parties, relaying and possibly altering their traffic while each believes it talks directly to the other.
example: A MITM on public Wi-Fi could relay an SSH connection if the user ignores a changed host key.

definition: An independent logical stream multiplexed over one SSH connection, used for a shell, a command, a subsystem such as SFTP or a forwarded port. Each has its own flow-control window.
example: One SSH connection can carry a shell channel and two port-forward channels at once.

definition: A named service started inside an SSH session channel, such as sftp, instead of a shell or command.
example: The sftp client requests the sftp subsystem after opening a session channel.

definition: Relaying TCP connections through an SSH connection. ssh -L forwards a local port to a remote destination (a direct-tcpip channel); ssh -R forwards a port on the server back to you.
example: ssh -L 5432:db.internal:5432 bastion lets a local client reach a database behind the bastion.

definition: The number of bytes an SSH channel's sender may still send before the receiver grants more with CHANNEL_WINDOW_ADJUST. A small window limits throughput to about window ÷ RTT.
example: Under an ideal prompt-credit model, a 2 MiB window and 100 ms feedback round trip give a ceiling of about 168 Mbit/s; other limits can lower throughput.

definition: High Performance SSH: a patched OpenSSH that enlarges channel windows and buffers so bulk transfers run faster over high-latency links.
example: HPN-SSH is used by research networks moving terabytes between continents.

definition: SSH File Transfer Protocol: a binary protocol for remote file access that runs as the sftp subsystem inside one SSH channel. It is unrelated to FTP apart from the name.
example: sftp user@host opens, reads and writes files over port 22 with no extra connections.

definition: File Transfer Protocol: an old plaintext protocol that uses one TCP connection for commands and separate connections for each data transfer, which makes it awkward through firewalls and NAT.
example: FTP's control connection uses port 21, while each file listing opens another data connection.

definition: FTP protected using TLS, distinct from SFTP over SSH. RFC 4217 describes explicit TLS negotiation on the FTP control connection; implicit FTPS commonly uses a separately configured port such as 990.
example: A legacy bank file exchange may use FTPS on port 990.

definition: A command for copying files over SSH. Since OpenSSH 9.0 it uses the SFTP protocol by default instead of its original rcp-derived protocol.
example: scp report.pdf host:/tmp/ copies a file to /tmp on host.

definition: The SFTP message types, such as SSH_FXP_OPEN, READ, WRITE, DATA and CLOSE. Each file-operation request carries an ID so many can be outstanding at once; INIT and VERSION negotiate the protocol version first.
example: A client sends SSH_FXP_READ id=2 for 32,768 bytes at offset 0 and receives SSH_FXP_DATA id=2.

definition: An opaque token a server returns when a file is opened, used to refer to that open file in later read, write and close requests.
example: After SSH_FXP_OPEN the server replies with a handle, and every READ quotes it.

definition: A number a client attaches to each request so replies can be matched to requests even when they arrive in a different order, allowing many requests to be in flight at once. SFTP requests carry IDs; HTTP/1.1 has none, so it must return responses in request order.
example: SFTP READs with IDs 2, 3 and 4 can all be outstanding; replies say which ID they answer.

definition: 1,024 bytes (2^10). The 'i' marks a binary unit, unlike the kilobyte (kB) of 1,000 bytes.
example: A 32 KiB SFTP read is 32 × 1,024 = 32,768 bytes.
64 outstanding 32 KiB reads total 2 MiB.
1 GiB divided into 32 KiB reads is 32,768 reads.

definition: A data rate of one million bits per second. Divide by 8 for megabytes per second.
example: 400 KiB/s = 409,600 bytes/s × 8 ≈ 3.3 Mbit/s.

definition: A variant of gRPC for browsers, which cannot read HTTP/2 trailers through fetch. It moves the status into the response body and needs a proxy such as Envoy, or server support, to translate.
example: A web app calls a gRPC backend via an Envoy proxy speaking gRPC-Web.

definition: Google's compact binary format for structured data, defined by a .proto schema. gRPC uses it by default to encode request and response messages.
example: The message {id: 150, name: "hi"} encodes as 7 bytes: 08 96 01 12 02 68 69.

definition: The integer before a protobuf field value that combines the field number and wire type. Multiplying the field number by eight and adding the three-bit wire type forms the tag, which is itself encoded as a varint.
example: Field 1 with wire type 0 gives tag 0x08; field 2 with wire type 2 gives 0x12.

definition: The number assigned to each field in a protobuf schema, such as id = 1. It, not the field name, identifies the field on the wire.
example: In int32 id = 1, the field number is 1.

definition: A 3-bit code in a protobuf tag that says how to read the value: 0 is a varint, 2 is length-delimited (bytes, strings, nested messages), 1 and 5 are fixed 64- and 32-bit values.
example: Wire type 2 tells the parser a length follows, such as 02 before "hi".

definition: Protobuf's variable-length integer: 7 bits of value per byte, least significant group first, with the top bit set on every byte except the last. Small numbers take one byte.
example: 150 encodes as 96 01: 0x16 (22) with the continuation bit, then 1 × 128.

definition: Encoded with its length first and then exactly that many bytes, so a reader knows where it ends without a terminator.
example: gRPC prefixes each message with its 4-byte length; protobuf strings are length-delimited.

definition: The five bytes before each native gRPC message inside HTTP/2 DATA: a one-byte compressed flag and a four-byte big-endian length. The length counts the following encoded message bytes, compressed when the flag is one, and excludes the five-byte prefix.
example: A 7-byte uncompressed message is prefixed with 00 00 00 00 07.

definition: Storing a multi-byte number with its most significant byte first. Network protocols conventionally use it, which is why it is called network byte order.
example: The 32-bit length 7 is written 00 00 00 07 in big-endian.

definition: Storing a multi-byte number with its least significant byte first, as x86 processors do in memory.
example: The 16-bit value 5 is 05 00 in little-endian but 00 05 in big-endian.

definition: An unsigned 32-bit integer: a whole number from 0 to 4,294,967,295 (2^32 − 1). uint64 is the 64-bit equivalent.
example: gRPC's message length is a uint32, so one message can in principle be up to about 4 GB.

definition: A protobuf (and general) signed 32-bit integer type, from −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. In protobuf, negative int32 values are sign-extended to 10-byte varints.
example: int32 id = -1 takes 10 bytes on the wire.

definition: A protobuf mapping used by the sint32 and sint64 types that interleaves negative and positive numbers (0, −1, 1, −2 → 0, 1, 2, 3) so small negative values get short varints.
example: sint32 value −1 becomes 1 and encodes as the single byte 01.

definition: The time by which a gRPC call must complete. Native gRPC sends an optional remaining duration in grpc-timeout; the client can report DEADLINE_EXCEEDED even after the server committed work, and the server may not send that same status.
example: grpc-timeout: 250m means 250 milliseconds remain.

definition: Passing the remaining time budget to downstream calls, so services stop work the original caller has already given up on.
example: With 300 ms allowed and 50 ms used, a service gives its downstream call about 250 ms.

definition: The trailer field carrying a gRPC call's numeric result (0 OK, 3 INVALID_ARGUMENT, 4 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, 5 NOT_FOUND, 8 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, 13 INTERNAL, 14 UNAVAILABLE), with grpc-message giving optional text.
example: An HTTP 200 response can still end with grpc-status: 14, meaning UNAVAILABLE.

definition: gRPC status code 0: the call succeeded.
example: A trailer of grpc-status: 0 reports OK.

definition: gRPC status code 3: the client sent a bad request, so retrying unchanged will not help.
example: A trailer of grpc-status: 3 reports INVALID_ARGUMENT.

definition: gRPC status code 4: the deadline passed before the call completed; the server may still have done the work.
example: A trailer of grpc-status: 4 reports DEADLINE_EXCEEDED.

definition: gRPC status code 5: a requested entity does not exist.
example: A trailer of grpc-status: 5 reports NOT_FOUND.

definition: gRPC status code 8: a quota or resource such as a message-size limit was exceeded.
example: A trailer of grpc-status: 8 reports RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.

definition: gRPC status code 13: a serious internal error, such as a broken invariant in the server or library.
example: A trailer of grpc-status: 13 reports INTERNAL.

definition: gRPC status code 14: the service is temporarily unreachable, often a transient condition worth retrying if safe.
example: A trailer of grpc-status: 14 reports UNAVAILABLE.

definition: A gRPC response made of a single HEADERS frame carrying both the HTTP status and grpc-status, used when a call fails before sending any message.
example: A call to an unknown method can get a Trailers-Only reply with grpc-status 12 (UNIMPLEMENTED).

definition: A request header gRPC clients send to tell intermediaries they accept trailer fields, which gRPC needs for its status.
example: Every gRPC request carries te: trailers alongside content-type application/grpc.

definition: The content type that marks an HTTP/2 request or response as a gRPC call.
example: Proxies can route gRPC traffic by matching content-type: application/grpc.

definition: A gRPC call in which the client, the server or both send a sequence of messages on one HTTP/2 stream instead of one message each.
example: A price-feed method can stream thousands of updates over a single call.

definition: HTTP/2 PING-based checking of a gRPC connection, subject to client and server policy. It can help detect a broken path or retain some middlebox state, but does not establish application health or guarantee an idle connection survives.
example: A gRPC client may ping every 30 seconds if the server's policy allows it.

definition: An HTTP/2 error code a server sends, for example in GOAWAY, when a peer is generating excessive load. gRPC servers use it with debug data too_many_pings for over-eager keepalives.
example: A client pinging every second may be disconnected with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM.

definition: An open-source layer-7 proxy that understands HTTP/2 and gRPC, so it can balance each call (stream) separately across backends.
example: An appropriately configured HTTP/2-aware Envoy deployment can select an upstream for each gRPC call; configuration determines its balancing policy.

definition: The client itself keeps connections to several backends and spreads calls among them, instead of relying on a proxy.
example: A gRPC channel configured with round_robin opens a connection to each backend and alternates calls.

definition: Describes a service that another service calls while handling a request; the caller is upstream.
example: If A calls B, B is downstream of A.

definition: A design in which participants (peers) both use and provide data or resources, rather than all talking to central servers.
example: In BitTorrent, each downloader also uploads pieces to other peers.

definition: A design in which clients send requests to dedicated servers that hold the data or service.
example: A browser fetching a web page from a web server is client-server.

definition: A peer-to-peer file-sharing protocol in which a file is split into hash-verified pieces that peers download from and upload to each other.
example: A popular Linux ISO can download from hundreds of peers at once over BitTorrent.

definition: BitTorrent Enhancement Proposal: a numbered specification document for the BitTorrent protocol, such as BEP 3 (core protocol) or BEP 5 (DHT).
example: BEP 52 specifies BitTorrent v2.

definition: BitTorrent's simple serialisation format with four types: integers (i42e), strings (4:spam), lists (l…e) and dictionaries (d…e) with keys sorted by raw bytes.
example: {"cow": "moo"} bencodes as d3:cow3:mooe.

definition: The bencoded file describing a torrent: tracker URLs and the info dictionary with names, sizes, piece length and piece hashes.
example: Opening ubuntu.iso.torrent gives a client everything needed to find peers and verify pieces.

definition: The part of a .torrent file listing the content's name, length or files, piece length and piece hashes. Its SHA-1 hash is the info-hash.
example: Changing even the file name in the info dictionary changes the info-hash.

definition: A chunk of BitTorrent v1 content with a chosen nominal piece length and a 20-byte SHA-1 digest in metainfo. The final piece may be shorter; v2 instead defines per-file SHA-256 Merkle trees.
example: A 1 GiB file with 256 KiB pieces has 4,096 pieces and 81,920 bytes of hashes.

definition: A sub-chunk of a piece, normally 16 KiB, that is the unit actually requested from peers.
example: A 256 KiB piece is fetched as 16 blocks of 16 KiB.

definition: A cryptographic hash function producing a 20-byte (160-bit) digest. It is no longer collision-resistant, so new designs use SHA-256.
example: BitTorrent v1 stores a 20-byte SHA-1 for every piece.

definition: A cryptographic hash function producing a 32-byte (256-bit) digest, currently considered secure.
example: BitTorrent v2 uses SHA-256 Merkle trees.

definition: A tree of hashes in which each parent is the hash of its children, so one root hash commits to all the data and any block can be checked with a short proof.
example: A 1 GiB file with 16 KiB leaves has 65,536 leaves, but proving one block needs only about 16 sibling hashes.

definition: The SHA-1 hash of a torrent's bencoded info dictionary (SHA-256 in v2), used as the torrent's identifier with trackers, in the DHT and in magnet links.
example: magnet:?xt=urn:btih:<40 hex digits> carries a 20-byte info-hash.

definition: A link that identifies a torrent by its info-hash, optionally with tracker URLs and a display name, so a client can fetch the metadata from peers without a .torrent file.
example: magnet:?xt=urn:btih:… pasted into a client starts a download.

definition: An HTTP or UDP server that returns lists of peers for a given info-hash. It coordinates peers but does not hold the content.
example: A client announces to a tracker and receives 50 peer addresses.

definition: Distributed hash table: a key-value lookup spread across many nodes with no central server. BitTorrent's DHT maps an info-hash to peers sharing it.
example: A trackerless magnet link finds peers through the DHT.

definition: A BitTorrent extension in which connected peers tell each other about other peers in the swarm.
example: After connecting to 5 peers, a client can learn 50 more through peer exchange.

definition: Micro Transport Protocol: a UDP-based transport for BitTorrent with delay-based congestion control (LEDBAT) that backs off when it detects queueing, yielding to other traffic.
example: uTP delay-based congestion control aims to yield when competing traffic increases delay; it does not promise an immediate response to every call.

definition: The first 68 bytes each peer sends: a 1-byte length (19), the string 'BitTorrent protocol', 8 reserved bytes, the 20-byte info-hash and the 20-byte peer ID.
A 20-byte identifier a BitTorrent client chooses for itself and sends in the handshake.
example: Many clients start their peer ID with a code naming the client, such as -qB4650-.

definition: BitTorrent messages by which a peer tells another it will not (choke) or will (unchoke) upload to it. Choking limits uploads to a few peers at a time.
example: A peer receiving unchoke may start sending requests for blocks.

definition: BitTorrent messages saying whether a peer wants pieces the other has.
example: A peer that lacks piece 7, which you have, sends you interested.

definition: The BitTorrent message announcing that a peer has completed and verified a piece, giving its index.
example: After verifying piece 812, a client sends have 812 to its peers.

definition: A BitTorrent message, sent after the handshake, with one bit per piece showing which pieces the sender already has.
example: A torrent with 4,096 pieces needs a 512-byte bitfield.

definition: BitTorrent messages that ask for a block by piece index, offset and length (request), deliver it (piece) or withdraw a request (cancel).
example: request 7, 16384, 16384 asks for the second 16 KiB block of piece 7.

definition: A BitTorrent policy of downloading the pieces that the fewest of your peers have, which spreads scarce pieces and makes you useful sooner.
example: If only 2 of 40 peers have piece 9, a rarest-first client fetches it early.

definition: BitTorrent's reciprocity policy: upload mainly to the peers that upload fastest to you, choking the rest.
example: Every 10 seconds a client unchokes the few peers giving it the best download rates.

definition: Unchoking one peer regardless of what it uploads, rotated about every 30 seconds, so newcomers with nothing to trade can start and better partners can be discovered.
example: A brand-new peer with no pieces gets its first blocks through an optimistic unchoke.

definition: A BitTorrent peer that has the complete content and only uploads.
example: When a download finishes, the client becomes a seeder for the swarm.

definition: All the peers sharing one torrent at a given time.
example: A popular release may have a swarm of thousands of peers.

definition: A BitTorrent strategy near the end of a download: request the last few blocks from every peer that has them and cancel duplicates on arrival, so one slow peer does not delay completion.
example: With 3 blocks left, a client asks all 10 peers holding them.

definition: A distributed hash-table design using XOR distance and bounded contact lists called k-buckets. Its logarithmic lookup analysis assumes suitable identifier distribution and maintained live routing information; churn and adversaries can disrupt progress.
example: BitTorrent's Mainline DHT and IPFS are based on Kademlia.

definition: BitTorrent's Kademlia-based distributed hash table, defined by BEP 5. It stores peer contact information associated with an info-hash using bencoded KRPC messages over UDP and a bucket capacity of eight contacts.
example: A magnet link with no tracker finds peers via get_peers queries in the Mainline DHT.

definition: Kademlia's distance between two IDs: their bitwise exclusive-or read as an integer. Higher differing bits count more, so a longer shared prefix means closer.

A nonnegative distance function that is zero exactly when its two inputs are the same, symmetric when their order is exchanged, and satisfies the triangle inequality. The triangle inequality means travelling through a third point cannot make the distance shorter than the direct distance.
example: XOR distance satisfies all three, so it is a true metric.

definition: The identifier, 160 bits in Kademlia and Mainline DHT, that each DHT node picks and that shares a space with keys such as info-hashes.
example: Contacts are ranked by their XOR distance to the target; a matching prefix alone does not prove one node is the nearest.

definition: A bounded list of contacts in a Kademlia routing table. The original distance-bucket model uses power-of-two XOR-distance ranges; Mainline DHT uses splitting identifier ranges and a capacity of eight contacts per bucket.
example: With k = 8, each bucket in Mainline DHT holds at most 8 contacts.

definition: The set of contacts a DHT node keeps, organised in k-buckets, used to find nodes closer to a target ID.
example: A Mainline node splits eligible buckets as its known identifier ranges fill; its actual contact count depends on population and maintenance.

definition: In Kademlia, the number of queries sent in parallel during a lookup; the paper suggests 3.
example: With α = 3, a node sends find_node to its three closest known contacts at once.

definition: The Mainline DHT's simple RPC format: bencoded dictionaries in single UDP packets, with queries ping, find_node, get_peers and announce_peer.
example: A get_peers query is a bencoded dictionary with a transaction ID and the info-hash.

definition: Mainline DHT queries: find_node returns nodes close to an ID, get_peers returns peers for an info-hash (or closer nodes), and announce_peer registers you as a peer.
example: A client calls get_peers, then announce_peer with the token it received.

definition: A value returned by a Mainline DHT node in get_peers and required by that same node for announce_peer. It is bound to the requester's IP to limit forged announcements of other addresses; it does not prove possession of the content.
example: A node rejects announce_peer whose token does not match the sender's IP.

definition: An attack in which one adversary creates many fake identities to gain disproportionate influence in a peer-to-peer system.
example: An attacker running 1,000 DHT node IDs near one info-hash can control lookups for it.

definition: An attack in which an adversary surrounds a node or key with its own identities so honest participants only see the attacker, letting it hide or censor content.
example: Placing many IDs closest to an info-hash can eclipse it from honest lookups.

definition: A BitTorrent proposal that ties DHT node IDs to the node's IP address, making it harder to choose IDs freely for Sybil or eclipse attacks.
example: Under BEP 42, a node's ID must start with bits derived from a hash of its IP.

definition: The continual joining and leaving of nodes in a peer-to-peer network, which leaves routing tables holding contacts that no longer answer.
example: High churn means many DHT contacts no longer answer.

definition: A well-known DHT node a new node contacts first to learn other contacts and join; it plays no special part in later lookups.
example: A new client contacts router.bittorrent.com to bootstrap into the DHT.

definition: A set of browser APIs and protocols that let browsers exchange audio, video and data directly, including NAT traversal (ICE) and mandatory encryption.
example: A video-call web app uses WebRTC so media flows directly between participants.

definition: The exchange of setup information, such as SDP offers, answers and ICE candidates, that peers need before connecting. WebRTC leaves the method to the application.
example: Two browsers pass SDP through the app's WebSocket server before media flows.

definition: Session Description Protocol: a text format describing a media session: codecs, ICE credentials, DTLS fingerprints and candidates, as a=… lines.
example: a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2 says payload type 111 is Opus at 48 kHz, 2 channels.

definition: The model in which one peer sends an SDP offer listing what it can do and the other replies with an answer choosing what will be used.
example: The caller's offer lists Opus and G.711; the answer picks Opus.

definition: JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol: the specification of how the browser's RTCPeerConnection API creates and applies SDP offers and answers.
example: createOffer() and setRemoteDescription() follow JSEP.

definition: A username fragment (ice-ufrag) and password (ice-pwd) exchanged in SDP and used to authenticate ICE connectivity checks.
example: a=ice-ufrag:F7gI appears in the SDP for each side.

definition: Interactive Connectivity Establishment: a procedure that gathers candidate addresses for each peer, tests pairs of them with STUN checks and selects one that works, even through NATs.
example: ICE may test a dozen candidate pairs and settle on a server-reflexive pair.

definition: An address and port where a peer might be reachable, of type host, server-reflexive, peer-reflexive or relayed, with a priority.
example: a=candidate:1 1 udp 2122260223 192.168.1.20 54400 typ host is a host candidate.

definition: An ICE candidate using the device's own interface address, such as a private 192.168.x.x address.
example: Two laptops on the same Wi-Fi can connect via host candidates.

definition: An ICE candidate for the externally observed mapped address and port learned from a STUN response. That mapping need not apply to every destination or be globally reachable through all intervening NATs.
example: A STUN response reporting 203.0.113.5:61234 supplies an illustrative server-reflexive address.

definition: An ICE candidate that is an address on a TURN server, which forwards packets between the peers when direct paths fail.
example: If both peers sit behind strict NATs, they may end up on a relayed candidate pair.

definition: An ICE candidate learned during connectivity checks rather than initial gathering: an unrecognised authenticated request source can create a remote peer-reflexive candidate, and a successful check can reveal a new local mapped address.
example: A NAT mapping seen only during checks becomes a peer-reflexive candidate.

definition: Sending ICE candidates to the other peer as soon as each is found instead of waiting for all, so checks start sooner.
example: Host candidates are sent immediately; srflx ones trickle in after STUN replies.

definition: One local and one remote ICE candidate combined into a possible path; ICE checks pairs in priority order.
example: Candidate priorities, local preferences and the pair-priority calculation order checks; host-to-host is not an unconditional first choice in every configuration.

definition: In ICE, one side (the controlling agent) chooses, or nominates, which working candidate pair will carry media.
example: The caller is usually the controlling agent and nominates the best valid pair.

definition: An authenticated STUN request sent over a candidate pair to see whether packets get through in both directions.
example: A successful connectivity check makes that candidate pair valid.

definition: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT: a simple protocol that tells a client what public address and port its packets appear to come from, and is used for ICE connectivity checks.
example: A STUN server at stun.example:3478 replies with your mapped address.

definition: Traversal Using Relays around NAT: a server that relays packets between peers that cannot reach each other directly. It costs server bandwidth for every relayed stream.
example: A 1 Mbit/s stream relayed once costs the TURN server about 1 Mbit/s in and 1 Mbit/s out.

definition: Attempting direct UDP communication by creating outbound NAT/filtering state and exchanging checks against candidate public mappings. Success depends on mapping and filtering behaviour, timeouts and policy rather than being guaranteed by simultaneous sends.
example: ICE checks establish whether a particular candidate pair actually works.

definition: The fixed value 0x2112A442 in every STUN header, used to recognise STUN packets and to XOR the reported address.
example: A STUN parser checks the magic cookie along with message type, length and other required structure; matching four bytes alone does not validate a packet.

definition: A STUN attribute encoding a mapped port and IP address through XOR with the magic cookie and, for IPv6, the transaction ID. This obfuscation avoids some payload-rewriting interference; it is neither encryption nor a guarantee against every middlebox.
example: Port 61234 is sent as 61234 XOR 0x2112.

definition: A random 96-bit value in each STUN request, echoed in the response so the client can match them.
example: IPv6 XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS also mixes in the transaction ID.

definition: An older label often used for endpoint-dependent NAT mappings, where the mapping can depend on the remote endpoint. A STUN-learned mapping may not apply to another destination, but the label alone does not prove every possible direct path fails.
example: Your NAT may use port 61234 to the STUN server but 61890 to the peer.

definition: The rule a NAT applies to decide which incoming packets may use an existing mapping, for example only packets from addresses you have already sent to.
example: An address-restricted NAT drops a peer's packets until you have sent to that peer first.

definition: Datagram TLS: TLS adapted to run over UDP, tolerating lost and reordered packets.
example: WebRTC peers run a DTLS handshake and check each certificate against the SDP fingerprint.

definition: A security profile for RTP/RTCP providing negotiated encryption, integrity and replay protection. Ordinary RTP headers remain visible; optional header-extension encryption and negotiated transforms affect details.
example: WebRTC media always travels as SRTP.

definition: Using a DTLS handshake to derive the keys for SRTP media encryption, so keys never travel in signalling.
example: After the DTLS handshake, both browsers export SRTP keys and start sending encrypted media.

definition: A message-oriented transport with multiple streams and reliable delivery in its base protocol, with ordered or unordered messages. WebRTC combines SCTP extensions for partial reliability with DTLS to offer configurable data-channel reliability.
example: A game can send chat on a reliable SCTP stream and positions on an unreliable one.

definition: A WebRTC channel for arbitrary application data between peers, carried by SCTP over DTLS over UDP.
example: A file-sharing web app sends file chunks over a reliable data channel.

definition: SDP negotiation grouping compatible media descriptions onto a shared transport. A BUNDLE group can include several media/data streams, but the mechanism does not require every description in every session to share one group.
example: With BUNDLE, audio, video and data share a single candidate pair.

definition: Sending RTP and RTCP on the same port, told apart by the packet type byte.
example: WebRTC requires rtcp-mux, so one port carries both media and feedback.

definition: A group-call layout in which each participant sends a copy of its stream to every other participant. This makes each client's upload grow with the number of other participants.
example: In a 6-person mesh at 1.2 Mbit/s, each client uploads 5 × 1.2 = 6 Mbit/s.

definition: Selective forwarding unit: a server that receives each participant's stream once and forwards copies to the others without decoding.
example: Each client uploads 1.2 Mbit/s and the SFU forwards it to five receivers.

definition: Multipoint control unit: a server that decodes all participants' streams, mixes them into one and re-encodes it for each receiver. It saves client bandwidth at a high server CPU cost.
example: An MCU sends each participant one composite video showing everyone.

definition: Sending the same video at several resolutions or bitrates at once so an SFU can forward each receiver the version that suits its bandwidth.
example: A client sends 1080p, 540p and 270p layers; a phone on 3G gets 270p.

definition: Secure Frame: end-to-end encryption of media frames on top of per-hop SRTP, so an SFU can forward media it cannot read.
example: With SFrame, the SFU still routes packets but holds no key for the video content.

definition: Real-time Transport Protocol: packet structure and timing/source conventions for media, commonly carried over UDP but usable with other transports. Its fixed header is twelve bytes before contributing-source entries, extensions, payload and any padding.
example: A 20 ms Opus audio packet travels as one RTP packet.

definition: RTP Control Protocol: RTP's companion that sends periodic reports on loss, jitter, round-trip time and timing, plus feedback such as NACK and PLI.
example: Receiver reports say what fraction of packets was lost since the last report.

definition: Voice over IP: telephone calls carried as packets over IP networks, usually with RTP for the audio.
example: Office desk phones that plug into Ethernet use VoIP.

definition: Television delivered over IP networks, often by an internet provider to a set-top box, frequently using RTP over multicast.
example: A broadband provider's TV service streams channels as IPTV.

definition: An encoder/decoder: software or hardware that compresses media for sending and decompresses it for playback, such as Opus for audio or H.264 for video.
example: SDP negotiation picks which codec both peers support.

definition: An open codec for speech and music that WebRTC implementations must support, although a call may negotiate another supported codec. The Opus RTP timestamp clock is 48,000 ticks per second, independently of the actual encoded audio sampling mode.
example: A 20 ms Opus frame advances the RTP timestamp by 960.

definition: A video coding standard also called AVC. Its RTP payload format uses a 90,000-tick-per-second timestamp clock; other payload formats define their own clock rules.
example: With the H.264 RTP payload format, a timestamp difference of 90,000 ticks represents one second.

definition: A 7-bit RTP header field saying which codec format the packet carries. Values 96–127 are dynamic and mapped in SDP.
example: a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2 makes PT 111 mean Opus.

definition: A 16-bit RTP header field that increases by 1 per packet, letting the receiver detect loss and reordering. It wraps after 65,535 and starts at a random value.
example: If sequence 6700 is followed by 6702, packet 6701 is missing.

definition: A 32-bit RTP field giving the sampling instant of the packet's media in media-clock ticks, not wall time. It starts at a random value.
example: At 48 kHz, two Opus packets 20 ms apart differ by 960.

definition: The tick rate of an RTP stream's timestamps, set by the payload format: 48,000 Hz for Opus and 90,000 Hz for common video formats.
example: One second of video advances the timestamp by 90,000 ticks.

definition: The unit of frequency: one cycle or tick per second. 1 kHz is 1,000 Hz.
example: A 90 kHz RTP clock ticks 90,000 times a second.

definition: Frames per second: how many video pictures are shown or captured each second.
example: At 30 fps with a 90 kHz clock, frames are 3,000 ticks apart.

definition: A 1-bit RTP header flag whose meaning the payload format defines; for video it usually marks the last packet of a frame.
example: H.264 marks the last packet of an access unit; loss or reordering means receiving that bit alone does not prove the complete frame is available.

definition: Synchronisation source: a 32-bit identifier chosen to distinguish an RTP timing/sequence source within a session. It is normally initially random to reduce collisions, and does not permanently authenticate a person or device.
example: Audio and video from one browser have different SSRCs.

definition: Contributing source: IDs listed in an RTP header when a mixer combined several streams, naming the original sources (up to 15). CC gives the count.
example: A conference mixer's packet lists the SSRCs of the three people speaking as CSRCs.

definition: An RTP intermediary that combines several incoming streams into one new stream, listing the originals as CSRCs.
example: An audio conferencing bridge mixes everyone's voice into one stream.

definition: The first RTP byte holds the version (V, 2 bits, always 2), padding flag (P), header-extension flag (X) and CSRC count (CC, 4 bits).
example: Byte 0x80 means V=2, P=0, X=0, CC=0.

definition: An RTCP report from a media sender that pairs its current RTP timestamp with wall-clock time in NTP format, plus packet and byte counts.
example: Receivers use sender reports to line up audio and video timelines.

definition: An RTCP report from a receiver giving fraction lost, cumulative loss, highest sequence number, interarrival jitter and the LSR and DLSR timing fields.
example: Fraction lost is stored in an eight-bit fixed-point fraction: a field value of 13 represents approximately 5.08% loss for the reporting interval.

definition: Playing audio and video so speech lines up with mouth movements. RTP uses sender reports to map each stream's unrelated RTP clock to a common wall-clock time.
example: Receivers use the timing relationship from sender reports to align audio and video; acceptable mismatch depends on the application and observer.

definition: RTCP's running estimate of how much packets' transit time varies, updated for each packet by adding one sixteenth of the difference between the latest variation and the current estimate.
example: Packets sent 20 ms apart arriving 15 and 25 ms apart show jitter.

definition: Last SR: the middle 32 bits of the NTP timestamp from the most recent sender report, echoed back in a receiver report so the sender can compute round-trip time.
example: A receiver echoes the middle 32 bits of the sender-report NTP timestamp; zero indicates that no sender report has yet been received.

definition: Delay since last SR: how long the receiver held the last sender report before sending its receiver report, in units of 1/65,536 second. The sender subtracts it to get round-trip time.
example: A 40 ms hold is reported as 0.040 × 65,536 ≈ 2,621 units.

definition: Negative acknowledgement: an RTCP feedback message asking the sender to resend specific lost RTP packets, useful only if they can still arrive in time.
example: NACK for packet 6702 asks the sender to retransmit it.

definition: Picture loss indication: an RTCP feedback message telling a video sender that the receiver lost picture data, prompting it to send recovery data such as an intra picture.
example: A PLI reports picture loss and can prompt recovery, but does not guarantee an immediate keyframe.

definition: A video picture encoded without inter-picture prediction. It can support recovery, but codec-specific random-access rules matter; intra pictures are often larger than predicted pictures rather than invariably so.
example: A PLI may prompt an encoder to send recovery information such as an appropriate intra picture.

definition: A WebRTC congestion-control algorithm that estimates available bandwidth from packet delay and loss and adjusts the encoder's bitrate.
example: Delay-based congestion feedback can cause an encoder to reduce its sending target; the response depends on the algorithm version, observations and implementation.

definition: A congestion-feedback design reporting transport packet receipt and timing across media streams. Packet-status ranges can include missing packets; reports do not necessarily provide an arrival timestamp for every packet on the connection.
example: The receiver reports arrival times for 100 packets in one feedback message.

definition: The number of bits per second a media stream uses, usually given in kbit/s or Mbit/s.
example: A 720p video call might use about 1.5 Mbit/s.

definition: A receiver-side queue that holds media packets briefly to reorder them and smooth variable delay before playback. A bigger buffer survives more jitter but adds latency.
example: An illustrative 60 ms playout margin can absorb some delay variation, but its effectiveness depends on packet timing and the buffer's policy.

definition: The latest useful playback time for a media unit under an application's scheduling policy. A packet arriving later may be discarded for that unit, although a receiver can sometimes use late data for decoder state or other purposes.
example: A late packet may miss current playout even though the transport eventually delivers it.

definition: Traffic entering (ingress) and leaving (egress) a server or network. Cloud providers often charge for egress.
example: A TURN relay has 1 Mbit/s ingress and 1 Mbit/s egress for each relayed stream.

definition: A bitwise operation that outputs 1 where two input bits differ and 0 where they match. Applying the same XOR twice restores the original value, which is why STUN can scramble an address with it, and Kademlia uses the XOR of two IDs as their distance.
example: 0110 XOR 0011 = 0101; port 54400 XOR 0x2112 is undone by XORing with 0x2112 again.

aliases: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
definition: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, a professional body that publishes engineering standards such as IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) and IEEE 1588 (the Precision Time Protocol).
example: PTP is standardised as IEEE 1588.

definition: The time needed to put all the bits of a message onto a link, equal to its size in bits divided by the link rate. It is separate from propagation delay, the time each bit takes to travel.
example: 152,500 bytes is 1,220,000 bits, which takes 1.22 s to send at 1 Mbit/s.

definition: An identifier for one session between two parties. In SSH it is the hash from the first key exchange, which is mixed into authentication signatures so they cannot be reused on another connection.

The time a server spends handling a request between receiving it and sending the reply. NTP measures it with two server timestamps and subtracts it from the round trip, so it is not mistaken for network delay.
example: A server that receives at 10.150 s and replies at 10.152 s has 2 ms of processing time.

definition: One message delivery within an SMTP session: MAIL FROM, one or more RCPT TO commands, then DATA with the message, ending at the end-of-data marker. One connection can carry several transactions.
The specification for carrying one codec in RTP, setting its clock rate and the rules for timestamps, the marker bit and how media is split into packets.
example: RFC 7587 is the RTP payload format for Opus, with a 48 kHz clock.

definition: An SMTP reply starting with 5 (5xx), meaning the request failed and should not be repeated unchanged. For accepted mail, a permanent failure usually produces a bounce (delivery status notification) to the envelope sender.
example: 550 No such user is a permanent failure for that recipient.

definition: Several separate connections opened to the same server at once so requests can proceed side by side. HTTP/1.1 clients use them to work around in-order responses; each costs its own handshake and congestion-control state.

The way computers store fractional numbers, as a fixed number of significant binary digits and an exponent. Most decimal fractions such as 0.1 cannot be stored exactly, so arithmetic picks up tiny rounding errors.
example: In Python, 10.152 − 10.042 gives 0.10999999999999943 rather than exactly 0.11.

definition: Audio or video with a playback schedule and limited delay budget. Data arriving after a unit’s playout deadline may be discarded for that unit, although late data can sometimes support decoder state or recovery; UDP and timely retransmission policies make different tradeoffs.

An address intended for globally routable internet communication, unlike private or other special-purpose addresses. Actual reachability also depends on routing and policy; documentation address ranges used in examples are not live public destinations.
example: The illustrative mapping 192.168.1.20:54400 to 203.0.113.5:61234 uses a documentation-only external address.

definition: HTTP/2 byte credit limiting DATA separately for each stream and the connection, on top of TCP receive credit and congestion control. Both available HTTP/2 windows must permit the DATA payload; stream settings and WINDOW_UPDATE have distinct roles.
example: A receiver can stop granting one stream credit while continuing other streams if connection credit remains.

definition: Sender Policy Framework (RFC 7208): a domain publishes a TXT record listing the IP addresses allowed to send mail using it as envelope sender. Receivers check the connecting IP against it.
example: v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.0/24 -all allows only that /24 range.

definition: A cookie stored without a top-level-site partition key in the context being discussed. This is distinct from an explicitly Partitioned cookie; browser privacy policy can still block or partition storage in other contexts.
example: Deleting the accepted unpartitioned cookie in the quiz requires matching its ordinary name, domain/host-only scope and path.

definition: A DNS negative answer meaning the name exists but has no records of the requested type. It is sent as RCODE 0 (NOERROR) with an empty answer section, unlike NXDOMAIN, which says the name does not exist at all.
example: An AAAA query for a name that has only an A record gets a NODATA answer.

definition: A resolver storing a 'does not exist' answer (NXDOMAIN or NODATA) for a while, so repeated lookups of a missing name or type are answered from cache. RFC 2308 sets the time from the zone's SOA record: the smaller of that record's TTL and its MINIMUM field.
example: A typo'd name looked up repeatedly is answered from the resolver's cache instead of reaching the authoritative servers each time.

definition: Start of authority: the DNS record at the top of a zone holding administrative values such as the primary name server, a serial number and timers. Authoritative servers include it in negative answers so resolvers know how long to cache them.
example: An NXDOMAIN response for new.example.com carries example.com's SOA record in its authority section.

definition: The last numeric field of an SOA record. RFC 2308 redefined it as the negative-caching time: a resolver caches a negative answer for the smaller of this value and the SOA record's own TTL.
example: With an SOA TTL of 3,600 seconds and MINIMUM of 600 seconds, an NXDOMAIN is cached for 600 seconds.

definition: The NS records (and any glue addresses) by which a parent zone hands authority for a child zone to that zone's name servers. A resolver follows delegations from the root downwards to find who can answer.
example: The com zone delegates example.com by publishing NS records naming example.com's name servers.

definition: An encoder option that sends no packets during silence. With Opus over RTP, the next packet's timestamp jumps ahead while its sequence number is the next in line, so receivers can tell DTX from packet loss.
example: During a pause in speech, an Opus sender using DTX stops sending 20 ms packets until the speaker continues.

definition: Low-level background noise a receiver plays during silent periods when no audio is being sent, so the call does not sound dead.
example: An Opus decoder fills gaps left by DTX with generated comfort noise.

definition: In H.264 video, the set of coded data for one picture at one moment, which may be split across several RTP packets that share a timestamp. The RTP marker bit is set on its last packet.
example: A large keyframe access unit can span dozens of RTP packets.

definition: The RFC 9989 t= tag. With t=y, a domain owner asks receivers to apply one level less than its stated policy while it tests, so reject is treated as quarantine and quarantine as none. It replaces the old pct=0 practice.
example: v=DMARC1; p=reject; t=y asks receivers to quarantine, not reject, failing mail during a trial.

definition: An RFC 7489 tag meant to apply a DMARC policy to only a percentage of failing mail. RFC 9989 removed it because values other than 0 and 100 were applied inconsistently; its t= tag replaces the useful pct=0 behaviour.
example: Older guides suggest p=quarantine; pct=25, which RFC 9989 no longer defines.
